books.section: A. Farmers and the Populist Party
The Silver Issue and the Populist Movement

stimulus.text:
Mary Elizabeth Lease, a Kansas Populist speaker, in a speech around 1890. Lease made more than 160 speeches for the Populist cause in the 1890 Kansas campaign.

“Wall Street owns the country. It is no longer a government of the people, by the people, and for the people, but a government of Wall Street, by Wall Street, and for Wall Street.”
stimulus.source_note: Mary Elizabeth Lease, speech circa 1890 (Bill of Rights Institute handout; Gilder Lehrman Institute). Both quoted sentences are exact.

stem: Why would Lease's charge appeal to struggling farmers?

options.text: Farmers had grown rich by selling crops to Wall Street banks
options.misconception: Farmers faced falling prices and debt, not riches from bank sales.

options.text: Farmers blamed banks and railroads for debt and falling prices
Farmers wanted the government to buy their land at high prices
options.misconception: Farmers wanted relief from debt, not a government buyout of their land.

options.text: Farmers believed Wall Street would soon forgive all their loans
options.misconception: Lease attacks Wall Street; she never says it would forgive loans.

rationales.A: Falling crop prices left farmers poorer, not richer.
rationales.B: Debt and low prices made bankers a natural target for farmers.
rationales.C: The Populists wanted cheaper money and fair rates, not land buyouts.
rationales.D: Lease promises a fight with Wall Street, not forgiveness from it.
rationales.general:
Connect Lease's enemy to the farmers' troubles.
1. Background from the books: farmers in the 1890s faced falling crop prices and heavy debts.
2. Background from the books: banks held their mortgages, and railroads set their freight rates.
3. Lease names Wall Street as the power behind both.
4. A charge sticks when it names the power people already blame.
Remember: a speaker's charge works when it matches the audience's own troubles.
